quests.instruction: After a morning of heavy rain, Ishaan and his dad find a road covered in fast-flowing brown water on the way home.
quests.question: What is the safest choice?
options: Wade across quickly
Take another route on higher ground
Follow the stream along the road
Jump in to test the depth
quests.correctAnswer: Take another route on higher ground
quests.hint: Moving water can be stronger than it looks.
quests.explanation: Fast water can push people over and hide holes in the road, so choosing a different, higher route is safer.
quests.funFact: Even shallow, fast-moving water can knock a person off their feet.

quests.instruction: The class talks about heavy-rain safety and the stream behind the school.
quests.question: Why should children stay away from streams and drains during heavy rain?
options: The water is too cold to touch
Streams run dry after heavy rain
Wind can lift people off the ground
Water rises fast and banks get slippery
quests.correctAnswer: Water rises fast and banks get slippery
quests.hint: Consider how a small stream changes after a lot of rain.
quests.explanation: A quiet stream can swell within minutes in heavy rain, and wet banks are slippery.
quests.funFact: Culverts and drains can fill up very fast during a downpour.

quests.instruction: A flooded road stretches ahead, covered in muddy water.
quests.question: Which clue tells you to turn back instead of crossing?
options: The water looks a little wet
You can't tell how deep it is
The Sun is shining again
A car drove through slowly
quests.correctAnswer: You can't tell how deep it is
quests.hint: What can't you see when water is muddy?
quests.explanation: If you can't see the road surface, you can't know the depth or what is hidden underneath, so turning back is safest.
quests.funFact: Many flood accidents happen when people enter water they think is shallow.

quests.instruction: On a very hot afternoon, Zara feels dizzy and has a headache while playing outside.
quests.question: What should she do?
options: Put on a thick jumper to warm up
Keep running until she feels better
Go to shade, drink water, tell an adult
Play a bit harder to burn it off
quests.correctAnswer: Go to shade, drink water, tell an adult
quests.hint: Her body is telling her it is too hot.
quests.explanation: Dizziness in the heat is a signal to cool down, rest in shade, drink water and let an adult know.
quests.funFact: Feeling very tired or dizzy in the heat is a signal to rest.

quests.instruction: A news reporter reminds families never to leave anyone sitting in a parked car on a hot day.
quests.question: Why is a closed parked car dangerous?
options: It heats up faster than the air outside
It gets very windy inside the car
It fills with cold air quickly
It makes the Sun's rays much stronger
quests.correctAnswer: It heats up faster than the air outside
quests.hint: Picture sunlight shining through the windows.
quests.explanation: Sunlight heats the inside of a closed car quickly, so it can be much hotter than the air outside.
quests.funFact: A closed car can get far hotter inside than the outside air within minutes.

quests.instruction: On a hot day, Nikhil wants to know whether the pavement is safe for his dog's paws.
quests.question: How could he check?
options: Look closely at the colour of the pavement
Press the back of his hand on it briefly
Listen carefully for a sizzling sound
Wet his shoes before walking on it
quests.correctAnswer: Press the back of his hand on it briefly
quests.hint: If it hurts your hand, it will hurt a paw.
quests.explanation: If the pavement feels too hot for your hand, it's too hot for a dog's paws.
quests.funFact: Dark pavements can get much hotter than the air above them.

quests.instruction: In freezing weather, Leo's fingers start to hurt and feel numb after a long time in the snow.
quests.question: What is the best way to warm up?
options: Put them straight into very hot water
Keep playing outside
Go indoors and warm them gradually
Rub them hard with snow
quests.correctAnswer: Go indoors and warm them gradually
quests.hint: Warming up should be gentle and happen indoors.
quests.explanation: Going inside and warming up slowly protects cold skin. Very hot water or rubbing can damage it.
quests.funFact: Fingers and toes get cold first because the body protects its core.

quests.instruction: After a snow day, Mia's clothes are soaked through.
quests.question: Why should she change into dry clothes?
options: Dry clothes look more colourful
Snow leaves stains that are hard to wash
Wet clothes make you lose heat faster
Wet clothes weigh less than dry ones
quests.correctAnswer: Wet clothes make you lose heat faster
quests.hint: Imagine water and your body's warmth.
quests.explanation: Water pulls heat away from your body faster than air, so wet clothes can make you cold.
quests.funFact: Water carries heat away from your body many times faster than air does.

quests.instruction: A pond near school has frozen over, and a thin layer of snow hides the ice.
quests.question: What should the children do?
options: Stay off it unless an adult says so
Test it carefully with one foot first
Run across it quickly in a group
Throw stones to see if it cracks
quests.correctAnswer: Stay off it unless an adult says so
quests.hint: Ice can look solid in one place and thin in another.
quests.explanation: Ice thickness varies across a pond, and thin ice can break without warning, so adults must check it.
quests.funFact: Ice can be thicker near the edges and thinner in the middle.

quests.instruction: India's weather office uses colours to show how serious a warning is.
quests.question: Which colour means the most serious level?
options: Orange
Green
Yellow
Red
quests.correctAnswer: Red
quests.hint: Think of road lights: which colour means stop?
quests.explanation: Red is the highest level, meaning dangerous weather, so people should follow official advice closely.
quests.funFact: Colour warnings let people understand the seriousness quickly.

quests.instruction: The lights go out during a night storm and the family needs light.
quests.question: What is the safest choice?
options: A burning candle
A hot stove flame
A box of matches
A battery torch
quests.correctAnswer: A battery torch
quests.hint: Focus on what has no flame.
quests.explanation: A torch gives light without fire, so there is no risk of it tipping over or setting something alight.
quests.funFact: A torch is much safer than a candle during storms.

quests.instruction: Very strong winds are rattling the windows of the house.
quests.question: Which place in the house is the safest to stand?
options: Next to a large window
Under a loose shelf
Away from windows
On the balcony
quests.correctAnswer: Away from windows
quests.hint: Remember what could break or fly in.
quests.explanation: Strong wind can send objects flying into windows. Staying away from glass keeps you safe.
quests.funFact: Flying objects cause many injuries in storms.

quests.instruction: A warning says heavy rain will arrive tonight, and the class trip to the river is tomorrow morning.
quests.question: What is a sensible plan?
options: Check again and follow the teachers
Go anyway without checking the weather
Wade into the river to test the depth
Cancel all school trips for the year
quests.correctAnswer: Check again and follow the teachers
quests.hint: Plans can change when the weather does.
quests.explanation: Rivers can be unsafe after heavy rain. Checking again and trusting the teachers helps keep everyone safe.
quests.funFact: Changing plans because of weather is a normal part of staying safe.

quests.instruction: It is pouring on the way to school.
quests.question: Which action is the safest?
options: Run across the road without stopping
Wear bright clothing so drivers can see you
Hide behind parked vehicles until clear
Walk along the middle of the road
quests.correctAnswer: Wear bright clothing so drivers can see you
quests.hint: Notice how well drivers can see in rain.
quests.explanation: Rain makes it harder for drivers to see, so bright clothes help them notice you.
quests.funFact: Bright colours show up much better than dark colours in poor light.

quests.instruction: The family wants to know whether a big storm is really coming.
quests.question: Where is the best place to find official weather alerts?
options: A friend's guess about what the sky will do
Rumours shared widely on social media
The national weather office or trusted news
An old forecast that was left in a drawer
quests.correctAnswer: The national weather office or trusted news
quests.hint: Consider who measures and studies the weather.
quests.explanation: Official weather offices study data and send out warnings, so they are the most reliable source.
quests.funFact: India's national weather service is the India Meteorological Department.

quests.instruction: During a heat wave, a school keeps children indoors during the hottest hours.
quests.question: Why is this a good idea?
options: The Sun gets lost
Heat can make children ill
Children don't like sunshine
The school wants to save power
quests.correctAnswer: Heat can make children ill
quests.hint: Picture how a body copes with very high temperatures.
quests.explanation: Staying out of the heat during the hottest hours protects children from overheating.
quests.funFact: A heat wave is a period of unusually hot weather lasting several days.

quests.instruction: A forecast describes four hot days, and one will be the hardest on the body.
quests.question: Which kind of day is the hardest on the body?
options: Hot and humid with no wind
Cool and humid
Mild and cloudy
Hot and dry with a breeze
quests.correctAnswer: Hot and humid with no wind
quests.hint: Sweat has trouble drying when the air is damp and still.
quests.explanation: Humidity slows sweat drying and still air gives no relief, so the body cools less well.
quests.funFact: Humid air makes heat feel stronger because sweat dries slowly.

quests.instruction: It's noon on a very hot day and the family is deciding on an activity.
quests.question: Which activity is the safest?
options: A football match in the Sun
A running race
Climbing a hill
Quiet indoor games or reading
quests.correctAnswer: Quiet indoor games or reading
quests.hint: Imagine avoiding hard exercise in the strongest heat.
quests.explanation: Resting in a cool place is the safest choice at the hottest time of day.
quests.funFact: In very hot places, people often rest in the afternoon, like the siesta in Spain.

quests.instruction: There is shallow brown water covering a field path, and Vikram thinks he can walk through it easily.
quests.question: Why should he avoid walking through floodwater?
options: It might stain his shoes a muddy brown
It will probably be too cold to enjoy
It could make a lot of splashing noise
It may hide holes and strong currents
quests.correctAnswer: It may hide holes and strong currents
quests.hint: You can't see what's underneath muddy water.
quests.explanation: Floodwater hides hazards and may flow strongly, so even shallow water can be risky.
quests.funFact: Floodwater can also be dirty and carry germs.

quests.instruction: After a storm, a street is flooding because the drains are full of litter.
quests.question: What would help water drain away?
options: Adding leaves to the drains
Clearing the rubbish from the drains
Covering the drains with plastic
Painting white lines on the road
quests.correctAnswer: Clearing the rubbish from the drains
quests.hint: What is blocking the water's path?
quests.explanation: Clear drains let water flow away. Rubbish blocks them and makes flooding worse.
quests.funFact: Blocked drains can turn heavy rain into street floods.

quests.instruction: Water is slowly rising on the street outside the house.
quests.question: Where should the family go?
options: Higher ground, led by an adult
Down to the riverbank to watch
Into the cellar to stay dry
Beside the drains at the corner
quests.correctAnswer: Higher ground, led by an adult
quests.hint: Water flows downhill.
quests.explanation: Higher ground stays dry longer, and adults can decide the safest route.
quests.funFact: Moving to higher ground or a higher floor is a standard flood safety step.

quests.instruction: The class is learning about the Sun and a student asks about staring at it.
quests.question: Why should you never look straight at the Sun?
options: It is too far away
It can damage your eyes
It makes you sneeze
It makes the sky colder
quests.correctAnswer: It can damage your eyes
quests.hint: The Sun is far brighter than anything else we see.
quests.explanation: Staring at the Sun can permanently damage the eyes, even if it hurts only a little at first.
quests.funFact: Special eclipse glasses are made to block almost all sunlight.

quests.instruction: The family spends a whole day at the beach with sunscreen packed.
quests.question: When should sunscreen be put on again?
options: Once a week, at the weekend
Not needed, since once is enough
After the Sun has set for the day
After swimming or sweating, and often
quests.correctAnswer: After swimming or sweating, and often
quests.hint: Water and sweat wash it away.
quests.explanation: Sunscreen wears off with water, sweat and time, so reapplying keeps protection working.
quests.funFact: A higher SPF number gives more protection, but it still has to be reapplied.

quests.instruction: The children build a snow fort beside a busy road after heavy snowfall.
quests.question: Why is that a poor idea?
options: The snow melts faster beside the road
The road makes far too much noise
Drivers may miss them and cars may slide
The snow gets dirty from the cars
quests.correctAnswer: Drivers may miss them and cars may slide
quests.hint: Focus on how vehicles behave on snow.
quests.explanation: Cars take longer to stop on snow and ice, and drivers may not notice children near the road.
quests.funFact: Vehicles take longer to stop on snowy and icy roads.

quests.instruction: Parents put together a simple storm kit for the house.
quests.question: Which items belong in it?
options: Colouring pens and sheets of paper
A torch, water and first-aid items
A kite, string and a picnic blanket
A beach ball and a pair of sandals
quests.correctAnswer: A torch, water and first-aid items
quests.hint: Remember what helps if the power goes out.
quests.explanation: A torch, water and first-aid items help during a power cut or storm.
quests.funFact: Emergency kits often include a battery-powered radio.

quests.instruction: Strong gusts are forecast, and the teacher plans break time outdoors.
quests.question: Where should she avoid taking the class?
options: Into the library for a quiet read
Into the school gym for a PE game
Beneath tall trees or loose scaffolding
To the reading corner in the classroom
quests.correctAnswer: Beneath tall trees or loose scaffolding
quests.hint: Notice what could fall in strong wind.
quests.explanation: Gusts can snap branches or knock things over, so staying away from trees and loose structures keeps children safe.
quests.funFact: Branches can fall in strong winds, even from healthy trees.

quests.instruction: It's raining heavily at the bus stop and cars are splashing through puddles.
quests.question: Why should Neel stand back from the kerb?
options: Heavy rain can push people over
Puddles by a kerb are very deep
Cars can splash him and may skid
Kerbs become hot in the rain
quests.correctAnswer: Cars can splash him and may skid
quests.hint: Consider the road, the puddles and the vehicles.
quests.explanation: Passing vehicles can splash water and skid on wet roads, so standing back is safer.
quests.funFact: Rain-covered windscreens make it harder for drivers to see.

quests.instruction: A teacher lists weather hazards and actions, and wants the best match.
quests.question: Which pair is the best match?
options: Flooded road: turn back and use another way
Icy path: run across it quickly
Strong wind: shelter under a tall tree
Extreme heat: exercise as hard as possible
quests.correctAnswer: Flooded road: turn back and use another way
quests.hint: Picture what keeps you out of the hazard.
quests.explanation: Turning away from a flooded road keeps you out of danger. The other actions would add risk.
quests.funFact: A popular flood safety slogan says: turn around, don't drown.

quests.instruction: Aisha isn't sure whether the weather is safe for a planned outdoor activity.
quests.question: What should she do?
options: Ask a trusted adult before going
Ask a friend what they think
Guess and hope for the best
Try it and see what happens
quests.correctAnswer: Ask a trusted adult before going
quests.hint: Someone with more experience can check the forecast and warnings.
quests.explanation: Adults can check official forecasts and warnings, so asking them is the safest choice.
quests.funFact: Weather offices around the world share their warnings so that countries can prepare together.

quests.instruction: A class discusses one habit that helps in almost every kind of weather.
quests.question: Which habit is the most useful?
options: Wear the same clothes daily
Stay home on cloudy days
Carry a snow shovel
Check the forecast first
quests.correctAnswer: Check the forecast first
quests.hint: It tells you what to expect before you step outside.
quests.explanation: Checking the forecast helps you plan clothing, travel and activities for any kind of weather.
quests.funFact: Modern forecasts use supercomputers to calculate how air will move.
